rows.name: The Abecedarian trial’s age-30 outcomes justify expanding programs modeled on it.
rows.description: This policy position weighs ABC’s age-30 education and employment findings against its non-significant primary income-to-needs result. One small historical trial does not resolve modern program design, cost, delivery, scale, or priority choices.

rows.name: At age 30, 88.46% of ABC-treated participants versus 81.63% of controls had a high-school diploma or GED.
rows.description: The difference was not statistically significant (OR 1.73; 95% CI 0.57–5.27; p=.34) in the 52-treated/49-control ABC follow-up. This is a secondary education outcome, not a separate trial or evidence of a degree effect.

rows.name: At age 30, 3.85% of ABC-treated participants versus 20.41% of controls used public aid at least 10% of the observed window.
rows.description: The source reports OR 0.16 (95% CI 0.03–0.75; p=.02) for this ABC randomized-treatment comparison. It is a threshold for administrative welfare use, not a measured income or lifetime benefit.

rows.name: At age 30, ABC-treated participants had their first parity 1.83 years later on average than controls (21.78 versus 19.95 years).
rows.description: The source reports d=0.52 (95% CI 0.19–3.45; p=.03) in the 52-treated/49-control follow-up. This is a secondary family-demographic outcome, not a measure of educational attainment or employment.

rows.name: At age 30, ABC treatment did not produce a statistically significant difference in criminal conviction (27.45% versus 28.57%).
rows.description: The source reports OR 0.95 (95% CI 0.40–2.27; p=.90) in the 52-treated/49-control follow-up. This does not establish no crime effect; it is one self-reported age-30 outcome in a small historical trial.

rows.description: In the ABC randomized treatment comparison, the age-30 outcome was F(1,99)=9.60, p<.01, d=0.62, with a 95% CI of 0.42 to 1.90 years. The analysis used 52 treated and 49 control participants and is ABC-only, not pooled ABC/CARE evidence.

rows.name: At age 30, ABC treatment did not produce a statistically significant difference in income-to-needs ratio (3.11 vs 2.22).
rows.description: The selected primary economic outcome had F(1,99)=1.61, p=.21, d=0.25 in 52 treated and 49 control participants. This does not establish no economic effect; it is one age-30, self-reported household-income measure.

rows.name: The ASAP Ohio Demonstration randomly assigned 1,501 low-income community-college students to program or usual services.
rows.description: The 2015–2016 Ohio replication covered Cincinnati State, Cuyahoga, and Lorain County community colleges. The program group had 806 students and the control group had 695; this is a replication of the CUNY ASAP model, not the original New York City trial.

rows.name: After eight years, ASAP Ohio increased degree receipt by 15 percentage points (46% versus 31%).
rows.description: This full-sample randomized estimate covers degree receipt after eight years. It is evidence from the Ohio replication and must remain distinct from the original CUNY trial’s completion outcomes.

rows.name: After eight years, ASAP Ohio increased bachelor’s-degree receipt by 6.2 percentage points (17.6% versus 11.4%).
rows.description: The report treats bachelor’s-degree attainment as an exploratory outcome for the randomized Ohio replication. Ohio ASAP support ended at transfer, so this finding does not measure direct four-year-college services.

rows.name: In year eight, ASAP Ohio increased average annual earnings by $3,337 ($27,934 versus $24,596).
rows.description: The report’s Ohio unemployment-insurance wage-record analysis includes 1,482 of 1,501 randomized students and omits wages earned outside Ohio. The source does not state a price year, so this dollar difference is not normalized or used as a benefit-cost measure.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance increased on-time college enrollment by 8.3 percentage points (46.0% control mean).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is 0.083 (SE 0.030; p<.01; N=4,175), using a preschool-offer lottery as the instrument. It measures enrollment within six months of projected high-school graduation, not degree completion.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance increased ever high-school graduation by 6.0 percentage points (63.6% control mean).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is 0.060 (SE 0.030; p<.05; N=3,883), instrumenting attendance with the preschool offer. The administrative outcome is graduation from a Massachusetts public high school, not college graduation.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance increased SAT test-taking by 8.5 percentage points (68.5% control mean).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is 0.085 (SE 0.034; p<.05; N=2,559), among the paper’s tenth-grade-MCAS analysis sample. Taking the SAT is a preparation/participation outcome, not a score increase.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance had no detectable effect on stacked MCAS math scores (estimate 0.029 SD).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is 0.029 SD (SE 0.056; N=3,615) across observed grades 3–8 and 10. This imprecise null estimate is not evidence of zero effect and does not contradict the paper’s non-test outcomes.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance had no detectable effect on stacked MCAS English-language-arts scores (estimate 0.005 SD).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is 0.005 SD (SE 0.057; N=3,569) across observed grades 3–8 and 10. It is a standardized-test result and does not determine the study’s later educational-attainment outcomes.

rows.name: Boston preschool attendance reduced recorded juvenile incarceration by 0.8 percentage points (0.7% control mean).
rows.description: The 2SLS estimate is −0.008 (SE 0.005; p<.10; N=3,335) for an ever-recorded incarceration or Department of Youth Services placement. The paper treats this as a relatively imprecise disciplinary outcome, not a mechanism or general crime estimate.

rows.name: Public preschool should be judged on later educational attainment and behavior, not standardized test scores alone.
rows.description: This policy position weighs Boston’s null standardized-test estimates alongside its reported college, graduation, SAT-taking, and disciplinary findings. The lottery evidence is about historical Boston applicants and does not establish that every public pre-K program will have the same later outcomes.

rows.name: The Career Academies evaluation randomly assigned applicants in nine high schools and followed outcomes for eight years after scheduled graduation.
rows.description: The MDRC report draws on more than 1,400 young people, most Hispanic or African-American, in a diverse set of participating sites. It evaluates Academies that sustained their core features; scope should not be generalized to partial implementations.

rows.name: Career Academy group members earned an average 11% more per year than controls over the eight-year follow-up ($2,088 in 2006 dollars).
rows.description: The report attributes a total $16,704 earnings gain over eight years to the randomized Academy offer. This is a historical 2006-dollar labor-market result, not a current wage estimate or benefit-cost ratio.

rows.name: Career Academies did not show an overall advantage in postsecondary educational attainment over eight years.
rows.description: The report says both groups had high completion and postsecondary participation; this is an overall educational-attainment result, not evidence against the separate earnings finding or every subgroup outcome.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: Career Academy earnings gains were concentrated among young men: $3,731 per year (17%) over the eight-year follow-up.
rows.description: The report attributes this subgroup pattern to higher wages, hours and employment stability. It must not be applied to young women or the full sample as a universal subgroup effect.

rows.name: CEP exposure reduced monthly household all-food purchases by $10.65 for households with children.
rows.description: The post-exposure difference-in-differences estimate is -$10.65 (SE $1.457; N=4,498,537; p<.01). It is a household grocery-purchase result, not a student achievement effect or a program cost.

rows.name: A zero-to-100% CEP exposure contrast reduced monthly household all-food purchases by $38.76.
rows.description: The continuous-exposure estimate is -$38.76 (SE $11.54; N=4,369,278; p<.01). It is an alternate exposure specification from the same study, not an independent replication of the any-exposure result.

rows.name: CEP exposure reduced the study food-insecure-household indicator by 2.11 percentage points.
rows.description: The state-level post-exposure estimate is -2.11 percentage points (SE 0.581; N=569,293; p<.01), from a 45% reference mean. It is a household food-security outcome, not a claim about academic attainment.

rows.name: Eligible schools should expand universal free meals through the Community Eligibility Provision.
rows.description: This policy position weighs the studys household food-purchase and food-security findings against the limits of its quasi-experimental exposure design. The linked evidence does not establish academic effects or that every school is eligible or can implement CEP on the same terms.

rows.name: CUNY ASAP’s eight-year net educational cost was $13,838 per program-group member in 2019 dollars.
rows.description: This CUNY community-college perspective is the program-group minus control-group education cost over eight years. It is not a benefit-cost ratio or a cost estimate for Ohio ASAP.

rows.name: CUNY should continue investing in ASAP for eligible community-college students.
rows.description: This policy position weighs the trial’s higher associate-degree completion against its eight-year cost findings. The MDRC evaluation alone does not settle priorities, scale, or alternatives.

rows.name: Eight years after study entry, CUNY ASAP increased associate-degree receipt by 12 percentage points (52% versus 39.9%).
rows.description: MDRC reports this program-versus-control result for the original CUNY randomized trial. It is an eight-year associate-degree outcome, not a result for Ohio ASAP or a later CUNY follow-up.

rows.name: After eight years, CUNY ASAP’s average cost per associate degree was $9,162 higher than control ($84,087 versus $74,925 in 2019 dollars).
rows.description: This is MDRC’s CUNY educational-cost comparison per associate degree, over eight years. The report says ASAP was no longer cost-effective on this measure; it is not a benefit-cost ratio.

rows.name: The CUNY ASAP evaluation randomly assigned 896 low-income students needing one or two developmental courses to program or usual services.
rows.description: MDRC evaluated ASAP at Borough of Manhattan, Kingsborough, and LaGuardia community colleges. The full randomized sample has 451 program-group and 445 control-group students; this is the original CUNY trial, not an ASAP replication.

rows.name: After three years, CUNY ASAP increased degree receipt by 18.3 percentage points (40.1% versus 21.8%).
rows.description: The adjusted original-CUNY randomized-trial estimate has p < .001 in the 896-student sample. Degree receipt is cumulative at any college over three years, not a later earnings or benefit-cost result.

rows.name: After three years, CUNY ASAP students earned 8.67 more total credits than controls (47.68 versus 39.01).
rows.description: The adjusted original-CUNY randomized-trial estimate has SE 1.95 and p < .001 in the 896-student sample. It counts cumulative total credits over three years and is not a degree-completion or cost-effectiveness measure.

rows.name: In semester six, CUNY ASAP increased enrollment in a four-year college by 7.8 percentage points (25.1% versus 17.3%).
rows.description: The adjusted original-CUNY randomized-trial estimate has p = .0040 in the 896-student sample. This is four-year-college enrollment in the final semester of the three-year follow-up, not bachelor’s-degree completion.

rows.name: DCMP randomly assigned 1,411 Texas community-college students across four colleges.
rows.description: The individual-level trial assigned 856 students to DCMP and 555 to the traditional sequence. It evaluates the early DCMP version, not later corequisite recommendations.

rows.name: DCMP’s five-year net social cost was $790 per program-group member (2022 dollars).
rows.description: This social-cost difference includes DCMP, course-taking, and estimated indirect savings over five years. It excludes CAPR evaluation costs and is not a benefit-cost ratio.

rows.name: DCMP primary program components cost $1,380 per program student (2022 dollars).
rows.description: The component total combines Dana Center and college start-up costs plus two years of steady-state operations. It is a program-cost component, not the five-year net social cost.

rows.name: DCMP increased credential-or-four-year-enrollment by 2.5 percentage points after five years (32.7% versus 30.2%).
rows.description: The five-year outcome difference was not statistically significant, so it is not generalizable evidence of a long-term attainment effect.

rows.name: DCMP increased five-year college-level credits by 0.4 (30.7 versus 30.3).
rows.description: The five-year difference in college-level credits was not statistically significant. It does not establish a persistent academic-progress effect.

rows.name: DCMP’s reported cost per credential-or-four-year-enrollment was $3,450 lower than control.
rows.description: This source arithmetic reflects $73,240 for DCMP and $76,690 for control, but its underlying outcome difference was not statistically significant. It is not a confirmed savings or general cost-effectiveness ranking.

rows.name: DCMP’s reported cost per college-level credit was $20 higher than control.
rows.description: This source arithmetic reflects $780 for DCMP and $760 for control, while the underlying credit difference was not statistically significant. It is not a confirmed cost-effectiveness difference.

rows.name: Developmental-math reforms should show statistically persuasive long-term outcomes before broad expansion.
rows.description: DCMP’s randomized five-year follow-up found no statistically significant credential/enrollment or credit difference, alongside positive net social cost. Its lower cost per attainment is source arithmetic on a non-significant difference, not confirmed savings.

rows.name: Chicago’s double-dose algebra policy assigned ninth graders below the national-median eighth-grade math score to two periods of algebra coursework.
rows.description: The policy doubled math instructional time and also changed peer composition and pedagogy. Its regression-discontinuity evidence applies near the assignment threshold, not to every student or every implementation.

rows.name: The double-dose algebra study reports positive impacts on credits, test scores, high-school graduation and college enrollment.
rows.description: The published study’s regression-discontinuity analysis reports these outcomes for the targeted Chicago policy. The abstract does not provide one common effect size, so this record does not invent a scalar estimate.

rows.name: The double-dose algebra study found its largest reported impacts among students with below-average reading skills.
rows.description: This is a source-reported heterogeneity finding, not proof that reading skill alone caused the difference or that the result applies outside the threshold-based Chicago policy.

rows.name: AIR evaluated 2,458 applicants to 10 Early College High Schools using admissions lotteries in five states.
rows.description: The 2005–06 through 2007–08 applicant cohorts included 1,044 students offered enrollment and 1,414 not offered. The outcome estimates are intent-to-treat effects of an offer, not separate evidence from the report’s complier analysis.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: An Early College offer increased any college enrollment by Year 10 by 7.2 percentage points (84.2% versus 77.0%; p < .001).
rows.description: This is the intent-to-treat effect of being offered enrollment in the 10-school lottery study. It measures any postsecondary enrollment by Year 10, not degree completion or an effect for every Early College model.

rows.name: An Early College offer increased any postsecondary degree by Year 10 by 11.9 percentage points (45.4% versus 33.5%; p < .001).
rows.description: This intent-to-treat estimate covers any postsecondary degree in the lottery-study sample. It does not isolate a particular Early College component or establish a lifetime earnings effect.

rows.name: An Early College offer increased associate-degree or certificate attainment by Year 10 by 18.2 percentage points (29.3% versus 11.1%; p < .001).
rows.description: This is the intent-to-treat effect for associate degrees or certificates in the lottery-study sample. It should not be combined with the bachelor’s estimate as independent study evidence.

rows.name: An Early College offer increased bachelor’s-degree attainment by Year 10 by 5.2 percentage points (30.1% versus 24.9%; p = .037).
rows.description: This is the intent-to-treat bachelor’s-degree result from the same lottery evaluation and horizon as the other attainment records. It is not a separate replication.

rows.name: An Early College offer showed a 0.8-point difference in four-year-college enrollment by Year 10 (57.6% versus 56.7%; p = .744).
rows.description: The report’s intent-to-treat estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero for this outcome. It does not negate the study’s other enrollment and degree findings.

rows.name: AIR’s model estimated $57,682 in lifetime private and public benefits per Early College student (2017 dollars).
rows.description: This is a source-reported modeled lifetime value from estimated attainment differences and prior-return studies, not observed earnings. The preferred estimate combines $33,709 private and $23,973 public benefits.

rows.name: AIR estimated a midpoint additional cost of $3,819 per Early College student over four high-school years (2017 dollars).
rows.description: The source averages the midpoint yearly cost difference ($955) across six Early College–traditional-high-school comparisons. It includes school spending, college instruction, and incremental dual-enrollment administration, while some centralized costs such as transportation were not fully captured.

rows.name: AIR’s preferred model estimated a $53,863 net present value per Early College student (2017 dollars).
rows.description: The paper defines net present value as modeled lifetime benefits minus modeled incremental four-year cost. This is not a measured participant payment or a result from a separate experiment.

rows.name: AIR’s preferred model reported a 15.1 benefit-to-cost ratio for Early College High Schools.
rows.description: This source-reported model divides $57,682 in estimated lifetime private and public benefits by the $3,819 midpoint incremental cost. It is not an observed return or a universal estimate across Early College sites.

rows.name: AIR’s conservative model reported a 4.6 benefit-to-cost ratio for Early College High Schools.
rows.description: The source combines $34,834 in conservative modeled benefits with a $7,615 upper-bound four-year cost. It remains a scenario analysis rather than an observed rate of return.

rows.name: Districts should expand Early College High Schools when local partnerships can deliver their documented degree gains at comparable cost.
rows.description: AIR’s admissions-lottery study found higher Year-10 degree attainment after an Early College offer. Its separate six-site cost-benefit model is favorable but depends on modeled lifetime returns and has substantial site variation.

rows.name: ERO raised ninth-grade reading-comprehension scores by 0.9 standard-score points (effect size 0.09).
rows.description: The end-of-ninth-grade GRADE assessment result has p=.002, with 2,672 ERO and 1,912 non-ERO students. It moved the reported national percentile from 23 to 25; 77% of ERO students still read at least two years below grade level.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: ERO increased ninth-grade core-subject GPA by 0.06 points on a 4-point scale (effect size 0.07).
rows.description: The program-year school-record estimate has p=.002, with 2,937 ERO and 2,213 non-ERO students. It is a short-run core-course result, not a later persistence estimate.

rows.name: ERO increased ninth-grade core-subject credit accumulation by 0.6 percentage points (effect size 0.06).
rows.description: The program-year result has p=.017 and measures credits earned as a share of those required for graduation. The report says the statistically significant credit effect did not persist into the follow-up year.

rows.name: ERO’s follow-up-year core-subject GPA estimate was 0.04 points and was not statistically significant.
rows.description: The reported effect size is 0.05 with p=.061; the program supports ended after ninth grade. This is not proof of zero later effect, but it does not reproduce the program-year GPA result at the report’s 5% threshold.

rows.name: Supplemental ninth-grade literacy courses should be paired with continuing support when schools seek lasting academic effects.
rows.description: This policy proposition weighs ERO’s first-year reading, GPA, and credit gains against its later nonsignificant GPA estimate after the courses ended. The trial did not test a particular continuation model, so it supports a question about sustained support rather than a proven implementation prescription.

rows.name: The EWIMS evaluation randomly assigned 73 high schools in three Midwestern states for the 2014/15 school year.
rows.description: Thirty-seven schools implemented EWIMS and 36 continued usual practice; the report studied first- and second-year high-school students after one year. This is a school-level randomized evaluation, not a claim about every early-warning system.

rows.name: After one year, EWIMS schools had a 4-percentage-point lower chronic-absence rate than control schools (10% versus 14%).
rows.description: Chronic absence means missing 10% or more of instructional time. The source reports this model-adjusted difference as statistically significant after one year of adoption.

rows.name: After one year, EWIMS schools had a 5-percentage-point lower rate of failing one or more courses than control schools (21% versus 26%).
rows.description: The source reports this model-adjusted difference as statistically significant after one year of adoption. It is a course-failure risk result, not a graduation-rate estimate.

rows.name: After one year, EWIMS showed no statistically significant effect on insufficient credits for on-time graduation (14% in each group).
rows.description: This is the report’s first-year null result for progress in school. It does not establish that the exact effect was zero or rule out later changes in graduation.

rows.name: The EWIMS report found that implementation of its seven-step process was generally low and challenging in the first year.
rows.description: Schools more often reported using an early-warning system and dedicated team, but the report found no detectable school-data-culture effect and did not identify the staff actions causing the attendance and course-failure changes.

rows.name: Does the Head Start Impact Study support expanding Head Start?
rows.description: This policy question is open for debate. Linked factual Claims separate early outcomes and care access from the study’s limited sample-wide first-grade differences.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: In the Head Start Impact Study, children offered Head Start were twice as likely as controls to use a center-based program in spring 2003.
rows.description: This randomized-study finding concerns the early care arrangement produced by an offer of Head Start, not a comparison with no alternative services. The report includes Head Start, preschool and child care in its center-based category.

rows.name: The Head Start Impact Study found favorable cognitive and health impacts after one program year, with more significant findings for the 3-year-old cohort.
rows.description: The final report describes end-of-program-year impacts for the randomized access comparison. It does not justify treating every measured outcome, later follow-up, or implementation setting as favorable.

rows.name: By the end of first grade, the Head Start Impact Study found few statistically significant differences for the sample as a whole.
rows.description: The report follows children from program entry through first grade and reports this result for the randomized groups as a whole. It does not establish that every subgroup, unmeasured outcome, or later-life outcome was zero.

rows.name: The Head Start Impact Study compared Head Start access with a mix of alternative care arrangements, not with a universal no-service condition.
rows.description: About 17% of the 3-year-old control group and 14% of the 4-year-old control group entered Head Start during the first year; the report therefore distinguishes intent-to-treat access estimates from estimates adjusted for no-shows and crossovers.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: The ICPSR Head Start third-grade archive provides public documentation, while some data files require a restricted-data agreement.
rows.description: The archive separates public-use documentation from protected files. This is a data-access statement, not permission to republish microdata or a claim that every file is openly downloadable.
flags: Title may label a record rather than state a finding

rows.name: The third-grade Head Start follow-up found improved preschool outcomes across developmental domains but few impacts from kindergarten through third grade.
rows.description: The report summarizes the randomized access comparison over the full study period. “Few impacts” does not mean every outcome or subgroup was unchanged, and the comparison group had access to other care arrangements.

rows.name: The third-grade Head Start follow-up reports that modest early language and literacy effects left one impact in each age cohort by the end of third grade.
rows.description: This source-specific follow-up statement preserves the report’s cohort structure and its distinction between early effects and third-grade measurement. It is not a claim about unmeasured later-life outcomes.

rows.name: The third-grade Head Start follow-up found that social-emotional results differed by age cohort and by whether parents, teachers or children reported them.
rows.description: The report describes favorable and unfavorable findings for different reporters and cohorts. Do not aggregate these into one universal social-emotional effect or treat reporter differences as a contradiction without outcome-level review.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade ECLS-K Reading ITT impact was +2.23 points (p = .075).
rows.description: The 4-year-old cohort estimate is regression-adjusted and statistically significant only at the report’s 10% threshold. It is one third-grade cognitive outcome from the national randomized access study.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade PPVT ITT impact was +2.17 points (p = .246).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted vocabulary estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. It is not evidence of a separate trial or later-life outcome.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade WJ III Letter-Word Identification ITT impact was +2.11 points (p = .275).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted literacy estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. The source reports it for the same randomized access cohort.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade WJ III Applied Problems ITT impact was -0.43 points (p = .729).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted math estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. It does not prove a zero effect.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade WJ III Calculation ITT impact was 0.00 points (p = .997).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted math estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. A zero point estimate does not prove no effect.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade ECLS-K Reading ITT impact was -0.18 points (p = .876).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted literacy estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. It is for the distinct entry-age cohort within the same national randomized access study.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade PPVT ITT impact was +1.83 points (p = .146).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted vocabulary estimate is not statistically significant at conventional thresholds. It is not a separate trial.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade WJ III Letter-Word Identification ITT impact was +0.44 points (p = .818).

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade aggressive-behavior IOT impact was -0.34 points (p = .043).
rows.description: Lower scores indicate fewer behavior problems on this parent-reported measure. This is the participation-scaled counterpart of the published -0.23-point ITT result, not an independent effect.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade IOT impact on being in the normal emotional-symptoms category was -0.09 (p = .005).
rows.description: Lower probability of the normal category is unfavorable on this teacher-reported measure. This is the participation-scaled counterpart of the published ITT result and remains reporter-specific.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade peer-relations IOT impact was -0.21 points (p = .020).
rows.description: Lower scores indicate worse peer relations on this child-reported measure. This treatment-on-the-treated estimate is the counterpart of the published -0.14-point ITT result, not separate corroboration.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade social-skills-and-positive-approaches IOT impact was +0.34 points (p = .025).
rows.description: Higher scores are more favorable on this parent-reported measure. This treatment-on-the-treated estimate is the counterpart of the published +0.24-point ITT result, not a separate study.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade total-problem-behavior ITT impact was -0.50 points (p = .090).
rows.description: Lower scores indicate fewer reported behavior problems on this parent-reported measure. This suggestive result is one outcome from the same cohort and is not independent evidence alongside its IOT counterpart.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade total-problem-behavior IOT impact was -0.75 points (p = .090).

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade closeness-with-teacher ITT impact was -0.67 points (p = .060).

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, the third-grade closeness-with-teacher IOT impact was -1.00 points (p = .060).

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, parents reported a +0.27 third-grade ITT impact on time spent with their child (p = .001).

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, parents reported a +0.40 third-grade IOT impact on time spent with their child (p = .001).
rows.description: Higher scores are favorable on this parent-reported measure. This treatment-on-the-treated estimate is the participation-scaled counterpart of the paired ITT result, not independent corroboration.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade promotion ITT impact was -0.02 (p = .092).
rows.description: Parents reported promotion for 94% of the Head Start group and 95% of controls; lower promotion means more grade retention. This suggestive result is one school-performance outcome, paired with its IOT counterpart rather than independent evidence.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, the third-grade promotion IOT impact was -0.03 (p = .092).
rows.description: Parents reported a lower promotion rate under Head Start participation on this 3-year-old-cohort measure. This treatment-on-the-treated estimate is the participation-scaled counterpart of the paired ITT result, not independent corroboration.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, parents reported a -0.23 third-grade aggressive-behavior ITT impact (p = .043).
rows.description: Lower scores indicate fewer behavior problems on this parent-reported measure. The favorable result is one social-emotional finding and does not resolve the conflicting teacher and child reports.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, teachers reported a -0.06 impact on being in the normal category for emotional symptoms (p = .005).
rows.description: Lower probability of the normal category is unfavorable on this teacher-reported measure. The result conflicts with the favorable parent-reported aggression finding and must remain reporter-specific.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age four, children self-reported a -0.14 peer-relations impact at third grade (p = .020).
rows.description: Lower scores indicate worse peer relations on this child-reported standardized measure. It is not interchangeable with parent or teacher reports.

rows.name: For children entering Head Start at age three, parents reported a +0.24 social-skills-and-positive-approaches impact at third grade (p = .025).

rows.name: MSSI randomly assigned 514 eligible CCBC male students of color to program or usual services.
rows.description: The 2019–2022 evaluation assigned 304 students to MSSI and 210 to usual CCBC services. It evaluates a two-semester culturally contextualized course and support package; the control group retained campus services available to all students.

rows.name: MSSI cost $885 per intended program participant in real 2021 dollars.
rows.description: The spring-2019-to-fall-2021 average is an intent-to-treat service cost based on intended students, including those who did not enroll. The report says early persistence and completion impacts did not permit a cost-effectiveness calculation.

rows.name: MSSI increased first-semester ACDV-course enrollment by 10.3 percentage points (66.4% versus 56.1%).
rows.description: This full-sample first-semester transcript outcome is course enrollment, not overall college persistence. The reported randomized difference has p = .012 and standard error 4.1 percentage points.

rows.name: MSSI increased first-semester ACDV-course passing by 15.2 percentage points (43.4% versus 28.1%).
rows.description: This full-sample first-semester transcript outcome concerns passing the intervention-linked course. It does not establish a later degree or persistence effect.

rows.name: MSSI showed no statistically significant first-semester difference in credits earned (+0.3; 4.3 versus 3.9).
rows.description: The full-sample first-semester transcript result has p = .446 and standard error 0.4 credits. The source also found no early persistence effect, so this result should not be presented as evidence of completion.

rows.name: MSSI increased fourth-semester A/B/C grades in all courses by 7.3 percentage points (12.5% versus 5.2%).
rows.description: This cohorts-1-to-3 follow-up result has p = .048 and standard error 3.6 percentage points (N = 256). It is later course-performance evidence, not a persistence or degree-completion effect.

rows.name: Community colleges should expand culturally tailored supports for male students of color despite mixed persistence evidence.
rows.description: MSSI’s randomized evaluation improved enrollment and passing in its first-semester course and found a later fourth-semester grade effect for early cohorts. It found no significant first-semester credits effect, documented inconsistent implementation and pandemic disruption, and could not determine cost effectiveness.

rows.name: Federal test-based accountability should be judged as a math-specific achievement policy rather than a general reading reform.
rows.description: Dee and Jacob’s NCLB study reports fourth- and eighth-grade math improvement, including a 0.22 fourth-grade effect-size estimate by 2007. The same source found no evidence of fourth- or eighth-grade reading improvement, so the evidence does not support a general achievement claim.

rows.name: Dee and Jacob estimated that NCLB increased average fourth-grade math performance by an effect size of 0.22 by 2007.
rows.description: Using state-level NAEP panel data and a comparative interrupted time-series design, the paper reports a statistically significant fourth-grade math increase by 2007. The abstract reports no standard error and does not further define the effect-size scale; retain it as source-reported rather than automatically normalize it.

rows.name: Dee and Jacob found evidence that NCLB improved eighth-grade math achievement, especially for lower-achieving groups and lower percentiles.
rows.description: The source reports evidence of eighth-grade math improvement, particularly among traditionally low-achieving groups and at lower percentiles. The abstract does not supply a single estimate or standard error for this finding.

rows.name: Dee and Jacob found no evidence that NCLB increased fourth- or eighth-grade reading achievement.
rows.description: This is the paper’s reported null finding for reading in fourth and eighth grade under its comparative interrupted time-series analysis of NAEP state panels. It does not mean that every reading estimate was exactly zero.

rows.name: Charter students had 16 additional days of reading learning per year relative to matched traditional-public-school peers.
rows.description: CREDO reports this matched-growth comparison for 201415 through 201819. It is not a randomized charter-admission estimate.

rows.name: Charter students had 6 additional days of math learning per year relative to matched traditional-public-school peers.
rows.description: CREDO reports this matched-growth comparison for 201415 through 201819. It is not a randomized charter-admission estimate.

rows.name: CMO-affiliated charter schools had 27 additional days of reading learning per year relative to traditional public schools.
rows.description: This sector subgroup result comes from the same matched-growth study and is not independent of the national charter comparison.

rows.name: CMO-affiliated charter schools had 23 additional days of math learning per year relative to traditional public schools.
rows.description: This sector subgroup result comes from the same matched-growth study and is not independent of the national charter comparison.

rows.name: Stand-alone charter schools had 10 additional days of reading learning per year relative to traditional public schools.
rows.description: This sector subgroup result comes from the same matched-growth study and is not independent of the national charter comparison.

rows.name: The gap between the best and worst jurisdictional charter results was 109 reading-learning days.
rows.description: This is heterogeneity across 31 data jurisdictions, not an effect estimate for one charter school or student.

rows.name: The gap between the best and worst jurisdictional charter results was 120 math-learning days.
rows.description: This is heterogeneity across 31 data jurisdictions, not an effect estimate for one charter school or student.

rows.name: CREDO reports smaller learning gains for charter-school special-education students than for matched peers.
rows.description: The official NCSS3 release identifies smaller gains for this subgroup but does not print a numeric day estimate. This matched-growth finding is not a randomized charter-admission effect.

rows.name: Districts should expand charter schools based on NCSS3’s national matched-growth results.
rows.description: NCSS3 reports higher average charter-student growth, but its matched comparisons are not random assignment. Wide jurisdictional variation and the reported smaller gains for charter special-education students make local evidence material to an expansion decision.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice used admissions lotteries to estimate enrollment effects for 16,496 rising ninth-graders.
rows.description: The 2005–2008 applicant cohorts were analyzed using lottery outcomes as an instrument for SSC enrollment. This is one longitudinal evaluation, not independent evidence for each outcome.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice increased four-year high-school graduation by 8.2 percentage points (76.3% versus 68.1%).
rows.description: The six-year outcome brief reports this SSC-enrollment estimate for students applying in 2005–2008. It does not identify which SSC features caused the gain.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice increased postsecondary enrollment within six months by 9.5 percentage points (52.9% versus 43.4%).
rows.description: This follows expected four-year high-school graduation and uses the report’s combined NYCPS, CUNY, and Clearinghouse context. It is not a degree-attainment or earnings result.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice increased four-year-degree attainment within six years by 2.5 percentage points (14.7% versus 12.2%).
rows.description: The degree-attainment denominator is 14,646 students with the most recent degree data, although the evaluation sample is 16,496. The result concerns four-year degrees, not certificates or two-year degrees.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice showed no discernible effect on employment rates or earnings in the available follow-up data.
rows.description: The report says employment and earnings records are unavailable for the full sample. This is not evidence of no future labor-market effect.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice used $2,572 less in five-year direct-service expenditures per target enrollee ($57,246 versus $59,818).
rows.description: This experimental accounting comparison uses earlier cohorts and a well-defined control-school counterfactual. The report does not supply a common dollar price year and excludes some facility, partner, and startup resources.

rows.name: NYC Small Schools of Choice had $14,674 lower cost per high-school graduate ($77,780 versus $92,454).
rows.description: This source accounting result combines five-year direct-service expenditures and 74% versus 65% five-year graduation rates for earlier cohorts. It is not a benefit-cost ratio and does not represent the cost of never undertaking the citywide initiative.

rows.name: Large urban districts should expand small, nonselective high-school options when lottery evidence shows sustained attainment gains.
rows.description: New York City SSC enrollment raised graduation, immediate college enrollment, and six-year four-year-degree attainment in a lottery-based evaluation. Earlier cost accounting favored SSCs per graduate but lacks a common price year and complete resource accounting.

rows.name: Kingsborough Opening Doors randomly assigned 1,534 first-time freshmen to a one-semester learning community or standard courses and services.
rows.description: The trial assigned 769 students to the program group and 765 to the control group. It evaluates this Kingsborough intervention, not every later Learning Communities or Opening Doors site.

rows.name: Kingsborough Opening Doors increased degree attainment at any college by 4.6 percentage points after six years (35.9% versus 31.3%; SE 2.7).
rows.description: This source-reported randomized difference is degree attainment at any institution after six years. It does not establish effects for other learning-community trials or settings.

rows.name: Kingsborough Opening Doors had a $3,580 higher total education cost per program-group member over six years (2011 dollars).
rows.description: The source’s accounting comparison is $33,990 for the program group versus $30,410 for controls. It is a six-year education-resource estimate, not a benefit-cost ratio or a general savings claim.

rows.name: Kingsborough Opening Doors cost $2,480 less per degree earned over six years (2011 dollars; $94,680 versus $97,160).
rows.description: This source-reported accounting output combines group-level education costs and degree rates over six years. It is not a benefit-cost ratio, a universal saving, or evidence for other learning-community trials.

rows.name: Community colleges should expand freshman learning communities when degree gains outweigh their added education cost.
rows.description: At Kingsborough, a one-semester learning community raised six-year degree attainment by 4.6 percentage points in a randomized study. Its $3,580 higher education cost per program member and single-college scope make broader expansion a contestable policy judgment.

rows.name: PACE randomly assigned 1,125 eligible Florida applicants across 14 centers.
rows.description: The 2013–2015 evaluation assigned 673 girls to an offer of PACE and 452 to referrals for alternative community services. It evaluates a voluntary, nonresidential, year-round academic and social-service package.

rows.name: PACE’s net societal service cost was about $10,400 per program-group girl (May 2017 dollars).
rows.description: The 12-month cost difference compares PACE and other services with control services. It adjusts PACE to a 7.9-month average stay, excludes participant opportunity costs, and is not a benefit-cost ratio.

rows.name: PACE increased days present in school by 9.8 in the first follow-up year (119.6 versus 109.8).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted Florida public-school administrative-record result covers the calendar year after study enrollment. It is an attendance outcome, not a graduation effect.

rows.name: PACE increased the high-school on-track composite by 13.4 percentage points (27.6% versus 14.2%).
rows.description: The composite requires absence below 10% of enrolled days, no expulsion or suspension, and no core-course failure. It applies only to high-school students and is not observed graduation.

rows.name: PACE increased credits earned as a share of credits attempted by 10.6 percentage points (77.5% versus 66.9%).
rows.description: This regression-adjusted academic-year measure applies only to high-school students in Florida public-school records. The report found no statistically significant difference in total credits earned.

rows.name: PACE reduced ever-suspended status by 16.7 percentage points in the first follow-up year (29.6% versus 46.4%).
rows.description: This Florida public-school administrative-record measure covers the calendar year after study enrollment. It is a short-term disciplinary outcome, not a later justice-system effect.

rows.name: PACE showed no statistically significant 18-month difference in girls incurring a juvenile-justice charge (+0.8 points; 22.0% versus 21.2%).
rows.description: The full-sample Florida juvenile-justice administrative-record difference was not statistically significant. A charge is the report’s juvenile-justice term and should not be relabeled as an adult arrest.

rows.name: States should treat PACE’s short-term school gains as insufficient evidence for statewide expansion.
rows.description: PACE improved several first-year school outcomes but showed no significant 18-month difference in juvenile-justice charges. The $10,400 net societal service cost and short follow-up leave graduation, delinquency, and full cost-effectiveness unresolved.

rows.name: Perry Preschool initial program cost: 17,759 USD per child (2006 prices)
rows.description: An undiscounted program resource cost per child, including operating expenses and classroom facilities. It is not annual expenditure or the financing-adjusted denominator for every economic scenario.

rows.name: Perry's economic returns are sufficient grounds to expand publicly funded preschool for disadvantaged children.
rows.description: This policy judgment favors expansion based on Perry's modeled long-term benefits. Whether those benefits would transfer to new programs remains a separate evidentiary question.

rows.name: Expanding publicly funded preschool for disadvantaged children requires evidence beyond Perry's economic returns.
rows.description: This policy judgment calls for evidence about the programs and populations proposed for expansion. It does not deny the positive returns estimated for Perry itself.

rows.description: Between 2006 and 2008, 207 people were assigned to Project QUEST and 203 to control; the report uses regression-adjusted intent-to-treat estimates. The evidence is specific to this health-care-focused support model and study sample.

rows.name: Nine years after random assignment, Project QUEST increased average annual earnings by $5,239 in current dollars.
rows.description: The full administrative-data sample contained 410 participants; the report marks this annual ITT difference statistically significant. Current-dollar earnings are not inflation-adjusted and are not a benefit-cost ratio.

rows.name: Project QUEST’s reported operating cost averaged $10,501 per participant.

rows.name: In San Francisco’s districtwide ethnic-studies expansion, enrollment increased science GPA by 0.199 grade points.

rows.name: Districts should consider well-evaluated ethnic-studies expansion when local evidence shows sustained GPA and course-failure improvements.
rows.description: San Francisco’s expansion study reports higher GPA and fewer course failures under student-level difference-in-differences. One district’s enrollment patterns do not predict effects of every expansion.

rows.name: Among Latine students in San Francisco’s ethnic-studies expansion, enrollment reduced any D/F by 11.7 percentage points.

rows.name: Texas Summer Bridge randomly assigned 1,318 students across eight colleges.

rows.description: The randomized Texas study found higher first-fall college-level math attempt and pass rates and higher writing pass rates. rows.name: Tutoring effects were stronger on average for teachers and paraprofessionals than for nonprofessional and parent tutors.
rows.description: Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan (2020) report this comparison in the meta-analysis abstract. It is an average subgroup pattern across heterogeneous experiments, not a guarantee for every tutor or program.

rows.name: Tutoring effects were strongest on average among earlier grades.
rows.description: Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan (2020) report stronger average effects among earlier grades. The comparison spans different subjects, programs and study settings and does not identify one universal grade cutoff.

rows.name: Tutoring conducted during school had larger average impacts than tutoring conducted after school.
rows.description: Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan (2020) report this setting comparison in the meta-analysis abstract. The result is an average association across experimental programs, not a cost-adjusted ranking of delivery settings.

rows.name: School systems should prioritize tutoring delivered during the school day.
rows.description: This policy position gives weight to the meta-analysis finding that tutoring delivered during school had larger average impacts than after-school tutoring. It does not establish cost, feasibility, staffing, or the effect of every in-school program.

rows.name: The 2024 tutoring meta-analysis estimated a pooled learning gain of 0.288 standard deviations.
rows.description: Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan (2024) report an overall pooled effect size of 0.288 standard deviations (SE 0.029, p < .001) across tutoring field experiments. Effects tend to be largest with teachers or paraprofessionals, earlier grades, at least three days per week and during school; the pooled estimate does not describe every implementation.

rows.name: Viking ROADS randomly assigned 574 eligible SUNY Westchester students to program eligibility or usual services.

rows.name: Viking ROADS increased SUNY Westchester enrollment in semester 3 by 8.2 percentage points (73.9% versus 65.8%).
rows.description: This is a semester-3 enrollment result within a six-semester follow-up. It does not measure degree completion or enrollment at every college.

rows.name: Viking ROADS students had 3.6 more cumulative credits by the end of semester 3.
rows.description: The source reports this three-semester credit-attainment difference during the randomized follow-up. It is not a cost, degree, or later labor-market estimate.

rows.name: Viking ROADS increased credential attainment by 11.8 percentage points after six semesters (35.5% versus 23.7%).
rows.description: The confirmatory three-year outcome is any degree or certificate at any college. The study was conducted at one college during major COVID-era disruptions.

rows.name: Viking ROADS increased earning 60 or more credits after six semesters by 4.4 percentage points.

rows.name: Sector workforce programs should demonstrate provider-specific, long-horizon earnings evidence before expansion.
rows.description: WorkAdvance’s four-site randomized evaluation reports pooled earnings gains but uneven provider-specific results. Its net-gain models depend on provider, accounting perspective, and horizon, so they do not justify a universal expansion or a cross-site ranking.

rows.name: Workforce agencies should expand Year Up-style training and internships when they can sustain the long-run earnings gains shown in the PACE trial.
rows.description: Year Up’s PACE trial found sustained seven-year earnings gains, while its employment-rate result was null and its cost-benefit analysis remains separately modeled. Expansion depends on retaining the multi-site program model and employer partnerships studied.

rows.name: Year Up randomly assigned 2,544 eligible young adults to program access or community alternatives in eight offices across nine cities.
rows.description: The 2013–2014 PACE trial evaluated six months of IT/financial-services training followed by a six-month internship. It is one multi-site study, not independent evidence for each follow-up period.

rows.name: Year Up increased average quarterly earnings in follow-up Quarters 23–24 by $1,895 (28%; $8,797 versus $6,901; SE $267; p < .001).
rows.description: This was the report’s prespecified confirmatory earnings outcome, using National Directory of New Hires records. The $ figure is reported in the source’s earnings table; do not treat it as a common-price-year cost or a benefit-cost result.

rows.name: Year Up reduced total earnings in follow-up Year 1 by $5,778 ($3,964 versus $9,742; SE $259; p < .001).
rows.description: The report attributes the early difference to treatment members prioritizing program participation over other work. It is part of the same seven-year earnings trajectory, not evidence from a separate trial.

rows.name: Year Up increased total earnings in follow-up Year 7 by $8,251 ($35,589 versus $27,338; SE $1,120; p < .001).
rows.description: This is an intent-to-treat Year-7 earnings difference in the same NDNH sample. It should be read with the Year-1 displacement and cumulative seven-year result, not as an independent replication.

rows.name: Year Up increased total earnings over follow-up Years 1–7 by $38,152 ($176,412 versus $138,260; SE $3,958; p < .001).
rows.description: This cumulative intent-to-treat earnings result spans the trial’s seven-year observation window. It does not establish lifetime earnings or the source’s separate cost-benefit model.

rows.name: Year Up increased the share earning at least $9,100 per quarter in Quarters 23–24 by 12.4 percentage points (44.1% versus 31.7%; SE 1.9; p < .001).
rows.description: This is a secondary intent-to-treat earnings-threshold result in the NDNH sample. It is not an employment-rate effect.

rows.name: Year Up showed no impact on employment at the six-year follow-up.
rows.description: The report says roughly 80% of both groups were working at the six-year survey and in Quarters 23–24. Higher earnings therefore should not be relabeled as a documented employment-rate gain.

rows.name: Three years after random assignment, Youth ChalleNGe participants were 16 percentage points more likely to have a high-school diploma or GED (72% versus 56%).
rows.description: This randomized ten-site result concerns diploma or GED attainment among eligible out-of-school youth. It is not a high-school completion rate for ordinary enrolled students.

rows.name: Three years after random assignment, Youth ChalleNGe participants were 7 percentage points more likely to be employed (58% versus 51%).
rows.description: This source-reported employment result follows a residential and mentoring program for eligible youth ages 16–18. It does not establish effects for other youth populations or delivery models.
